name: Query Planning and Joins
intent: Turn a declarative SQL query into the cheapest physical plan by estimating row counts from statistics and choosing access paths, join methods and join order.
scenario: A report lists every order placed by customers in one country: orders (20,000 rows) joined to customers (1,000 rows) with WHERE country = 'US'. The same SQL can run in half a millisecond or in several seconds depending on the plan the optimiser picks, and that depends on what it believes about the data.
problem: SQL says what you want, not how to get it. Even this one join can be executed in many ways that return identical rows but differ in cost by two orders of magnitude: scan or probe an index, loop, hash or merge, customers first or orders first. The database must choose before it runs anything, using only summary statistics, so every bad estimate becomes a bad plan, and a plan that was right yesterday can be wrong after the data changes.

howItWorks.title: Parse and build a logical plan
howItWorks.text: The parser checks the syntax, resolves names against the catalog and produces a tree of relational operators: scan customers, filter on country, join to orders on customer_id, project. This logical plan says nothing about algorithms. The planner then applies rewrites that never change the result, such as pushing the country filter below the join so fewer rows reach it, and flattening subqueries into joins.

howItWorks.title: Estimate cardinalities (row counts) from statistics
howItWorks.text: ANALYZE (or its automatic version) samples each table, typically a few tens of thousands of rows, and stores the row count, the number of distinct values per column, the most common values with their frequencies and a histogram of the rest. Selectivity is the fraction of rows a predicate keeps: country = 'US' matches 40% of 1,000 customers, so the planner expects 400. The join size is estimated as outer rows x inner rows / distinct join keys. These estimates assume columns are independent and values uniform inside a histogram bucket, which is where plans go wrong.

howItWorks.title: Choose access paths
howItWorks.text: For each table the planner compares a sequential scan (read every page, cost 1 per page in PostgreSQL's defaults) with an index scan (a few index pages plus one random heap page (the table's own data page) per row, random_page_cost 4 by default, about 1.1 on SSDs) and, if the index holds every needed column and the visibility map says the pages are all-visible, an index-only scan that skips the heap. A selective filter favours the index; returning more than roughly 5 to 10% of a table usually favours the sequential scan, because 1 random page costs as much as several sequential ones.

howItWorks.title: Choose join methods and join order
howItWorks.text: A nested loop reads the outer side once and probes the inner side per outer row: unbeatable when the outer side is tiny and the inner side has an index, ruinous otherwise (outer rows x inner rows comparisons without one). A hash join builds a hash table on the smaller input and streams the other through it: roughly linear, but needs work_mem (memory a query may use for hash tables and sorts) and an equality condition, and spills to disk in batches when it does not fit. A merge join walks two inputs sorted on the join key in lock step: linear when the data already arrives sorted from an index or a clustered table, otherwise it pays an n log n sort. With more than two tables the planner enumerates join orders by dynamic programming and switches to genetic or greedy search past about a dozen tables.

howItWorks.title: Cost the plan and execute it
howItWorks.text: Each candidate gets a cost: pages read (sequential and random weighted differently) plus CPU for rows processed and operators evaluated. The cheapest total wins and the executor runs it as a pipeline of iterators, each pulling rows from its children. The cost is a unit-less estimate used only to compare plans, not a time prediction; the useful number is how far estimated rows are from actual rows.

howItWorks.title: Read EXPLAIN ANALYZE and repair bad plans
howItWorks.text: EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan and its estimates; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs it and adds actual rows, loops, time and buffers per node. The first thing to look for is a node where estimated and actual rows differ by 10x or more: that is where the plan went wrong. Fixes in order of preference: ANALYZE after bulk changes, extended statistics for correlated columns, a composite or partial index that matches the predicate, rewriting the query (avoid functions on indexed columns, replace OFFSET paging, split OR conditions), and only last a hint or a plan override, which freezes a decision the data will eventually outgrow.

pros: You write what you want and the engine adapts to table sizes, indexes and data distribution, so the same SQL stays efficient as data grows
Cost-based choice beats fixed rules: nested loop, hash and merge each win in some regime and the optimiser picks per query
EXPLAIN ANALYZE makes the engine's reasoning inspectable: estimated against actual rows pinpoints the faulty node
Fixing statistics or adding one index improves every query that touches that data, not just one
cons: The optimiser only sees summaries; skew, correlation and recent changes it has not sampled produce wrong estimates and wrong plans
Errors compound through a join tree: a 10x underestimate at the first join can become 1000x by the third
Plans are not stable: an ANALYZE, a data change or a new version can flip a fast plan to a slow one overnight
Cost units are only a model: random_page_cost, cache hit rates and work_mem differ from the real hardware
Planning itself costs time and memory, which matters for tiny high-rate queries and for joins of many tables
whenToUse: Any relational workload with joins over tables of different sizes, where hand-tuning each query does not scale
Diagnosing a query that is slow in production but fast in development: compare estimated and actual rows node by node
Deciding which index to add: read the plan to see which scan or join the index would replace
After bulk loads, large deletes or migrations, to decide when statistics need refreshing
whenNotToUse: Do not hand-force join methods or orders (hints, enable_nestloop = off, join_collapse_limit tricks) as a first move: fix the statistics or the index and keep the planner's freedom
Do not tune from EXPLAIN alone on a toy dataset: plans for 100 rows say nothing about 100 million, so reproduce with production-sized data or copied statistics
Do not chase the lowest cost number: cost is for comparing alternatives inside one query, not across queries or machines
If a query runs once a month on a small table, the hours spent tuning cost more than the query ever will
pitfalls: Stale statistics after a bulk load or a big delete: autovacuum analyses only after a fraction of rows changed (about 10% by default), so a freshly loaded table can sit with the old row counts for hours

Correlated columns (city and country, order status and shipped date): the planner multiplies selectivities as if independent and underestimates by orders of magnitude; create extended statistics on the column group

Skewed data and parameter sniffing (the plan is built for the first parameter value it sees): a plan cached for a rare parameter value (3 rows) is reused for a common one (400,000 rows), or the reverse; look for generic versus custom plans and plan_cache_mode, or use OPTION (RECOMPILE) in SQL Server
Functions or casts on an indexed column (WHERE lower(email) = ..., WHERE created::date = ...) make the index unusable unless an expression index matches exactly
A composite index in the wrong column order: (country, customer_id) serves WHERE country = ? but not WHERE customer_id = ? alone; put equality columns first and the range column last
Reading only the top-line cost and time in EXPLAIN ANALYZE while ignoring loops: a node with actual time 0.05 ms and loops=400,000 took 20 seconds
Believing an index scan is always faster: for a filter that keeps 30% of the table, the sequential scan is correct and forcing the index makes the query slower
Fixing the symptom with a hint or a disabled join method in production code, which silently becomes wrong when the table grows 50x

roles.label: Parser and rewriter
roles.description: Checks syntax, resolves names and builds the logical plan, applying result-preserving rewrites such as pushing filters down.

roles.label: Cost-based optimiser
roles.description: Enumerates access paths, join methods and join orders, costs each from estimated row counts and keeps the cheapest.

roles.label: Statistics catalog
roles.description: Holds row counts, distinct counts, most common values and histograms gathered by ANALYZE; it is only as fresh as the last sample.

roles.label: Executor
roles.description: Runs the chosen plan as a tree of iterators and records actual rows, loops, pages and time for EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

roles.label: Tables and indexes
roles.description: The heap pages and index pages that the plan reads; sequential reads are cheap, random reads are expensive.

quiz.question: A team bulk loads 5 million rows into orders with COPY and, two hours later, runs a join report. The plan uses a nested loop that EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows estimated 3 rows and actual 400,000 rows, and the query takes minutes. What should they do first?
options: Disable nested loops with enable_nestloop = off in the application
Add an index on every column used in the join
Raise random_page_cost so the planner steers away from index scans entirely
Run ANALYZE to refresh the table statistics
quiz.explanation: A 100,000x gap between estimate and actual points at stale statistics after the bulk load, where autovacuum has not analysed yet. Refreshing them lets the planner choose a better join. Forcing a join method freezes a decision that will be wrong as data changes.

quiz.question: A 10-million-row orders table has an index on status, and 70% of rows have status = 'shipped'. A query filtering on that value uses a sequential scan, and a developer wants to force the index. What is the better call?
options: Leave it, since scanning most of the table is cheaper than millions of random reads
Run ANALYZE first, since a planner that picks a seq scan over an index must have stale statistics
Force the index, since an index scan is always faster than scanning the table
Add a second index on status so the planner has two choices
quiz.explanation: When a filter keeps more than roughly 5 to 10% of the table, random heap reads cost more than a straight scan, so the sequential scan is the right plan. Forcing the index makes the query slower.

quiz.question: A query filters WHERE city = 'Lyon' AND country = 'France'. Each column alone has good statistics. The planner estimates 20 rows, but 90,000 match, and a nested loop built on that estimate is very slow. Which change fixes the cause of the bad estimate?
options: Create a composite index on (city, country) so the filter is faster
Raise default_statistics_target so each column gets a much finer histogram and more samples
Create extended statistics on (city, country) to capture their correlation
Set enable_nestloop = off so the planner picks a hash join
quiz.explanation: The planner multiplies the two selectivities as if the columns were independent, but every Lyon row is also in France. Extended statistics capture that dependency. An index or a hint may hide the symptom while the estimate stays wrong, and finer histograms do not model correlation.
